e.t: This word describes an “obscure thing” or a “poor reflection”—something that does not give a clear, complete view. Its central idea is limited or imperfect perception: what is seen is real enough to resemble the truth, yet not fully clear. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Corinthians 13:12. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its meaning points to obscurity or an incomplete reflection.

d: The Greek way of writing the Latin Aquila, a male proper name; the husband of Priscilla (Prisca), and a Jew, of a family belonging to Pontus.

e.t: Aquila is a personal name, referring to a specific man rather than describing an object, action, or character trait. In the Greek New Testament, the name appears six times across Acts, Romans, 1 Corinthians, and 2 Timothy. Because it is a proper name, its meaning is primarily identification: it tells the reader which person is being mentioned. The surrounding passage is needed to understand what Aquila is doing or what is being said about him in any particular verse.

gl: to be moved by the wind
d: To be blown with the wind (referring to the gentler motions of the air).
me: Verb, Present, Passive, Participle, Dative, Singular, Masculine

e.t: This word describes something being blown or moved by the wind. It presents wind as the force carrying or shifting an object, rather than describing the object’s own deliberate movement. The word appears once in the Greek New Testament, in James 1:6, and its ordinary meaning is “be wind-blown” or “to be moved by the wind.” Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but the central picture is something unstable because the wind drives it.

This word means “an upper room,” referring to a room located above the main level of a building. It is a straightforward place-word rather than a description of an action, person, or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice: once in Mark 14:15 and once in Luke 22:12. The surrounding passage determines what happens in that room, but the word itself identifies its elevated location.

gl: to have nothing to do with
me: Verb, Present, Middle, iMperative, second, Singular

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb means “to avoid” or “to have nothing to do with” someone or something. It expresses deliberate withdrawal rather than engagement, describing what a person chooses not to associate with or participate in. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, at 2 Timothy 3:5. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense is a purposeful refusal of contact or involvement.

As an action word, it can refer to a spoken greeting when people meet, a respectful acknowledgment, or greetings conveyed through another person. It occurs 59 times in the Greek New Testament, showing regular use for ordinary personal greetings and respectful farewells or messages. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding words and situation.

d: Achim, son of Zadok and father of Eliud.

e.t: Akim is a personal name. In the Greek New Testament, it identifies a person named in Matthew’s genealogy. The name appears twice in the Greek New Testament, both occurrences being in Matthew 1:14, though the passage text is not provided here. As a name, Akim does not itself describe a virtue, action, or teaching; its meaning in a particular verse comes from the person and surrounding genealogy in which it appears.

Burden refers to a load or weight placed on someone, whether understood as something carried or as a responsibility that must be borne. In the Greek New Testament, this word describes something heavy that a person may carry or endure. It occurs six times across the New Testament, from Matthew through Revelation. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

This word means “little,” describing something small in amount, size, degree, or extent. It can modify a thing, measure, or period, helping readers recognize that what is being discussed is limited rather than great or large. The word occurs seven times in the Greek New Testament, including uses in Luke, John, Acts, and Hebrews. Its basic sense remains consistent: it marks something as little or small within its immediate context.

This word means milk, the nourishing food produced for infants and also used as ordinary food. In the New Testament, it appears five times and is used literally or as a familiar picture of basic nourishment. Its meaning remains simple at the word level; the surrounding passage determines whether the reference concerns physical food or uses milk as an illustration of early-stage instruction and growth. The word appears in 1 Corinthians, Hebrews, and 1 Peter.

e.t: This word means “to make clear.” It describes the act of bringing something into view or understanding so that its meaning, reality, or significance is recognized. As a verb, it can refer to something being made evident rather than remaining hidden or uncertain. The word occurs seven times in the Greek New Testament, across passages in 1 Corinthians, Colossians, Hebrews, and Peter. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being made clear in that surrounding passage.

This word means “foundation”: something that provides a firm basis or support. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Timothy 3:15. Its central idea is a stable base on which something rests or is established. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the word’s precise force in that passage cannot be explained beyond this basic meaning. Its lexical meaning is nevertheless clear: it points to a foundation or firm supporting basis.

e.t: This word means “to board,” “to go up,” or “to mount,” describing movement onto or upward to something. It can refer to getting onto a vessel or riding an animal, while in other settings it expresses going up to a place. The Greek New Testament uses it six times, all in six different verses, with five occurrences in Acts and one in Matthew. Its exact sense in a particular verse depends on what the person is moving onto or toward.

e.t: This word means “to put on” or “to rub on,” describing the action of applying something to a surface or person. It presents application as a direct physical act rather than merely possessing or carrying something. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in John 9. Its exact force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains the placing or rubbing of something onto another surface.

This word means “prosperity”: a condition of material success or well-being. It is a noun that names the favorable abundance a person or group may enjoy, rather than an action or command. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 19:25. The exact force of the word in that verse depends on its surrounding text; its basic lexical sense is prosperity.

This word means “half an hour,” referring to a period of thirty minutes. It expresses a measured span of time rather than an action, person, or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at Revelation 8:1. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the word’s basic meaning can be stated clearly, while its specific significance in that passage belongs to the wider context. Its single occurrence makes it a precise time expression rather than a broadly recurring biblical term.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to be dead” or “to die.” It describes the condition of death or the event of dying, depending on how it functions in a sentence. The word appears nine times in the Greek New Testament, referring to people who have died or are dead. It is used across the Gospels, Acts, and 1 Timothy, including passages that speak of a dead person, someone who has died, or the reality of death. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

e.t: This word describes carrying out sacred service, especially the work of serving in a priestly capacity. Its central meaning is “to minister” or “to perform priestly duty,” presenting the action as an active service rather than merely a title or role. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Romans 15:16. The surrounding verse provides the context for how this sacred service is being described, but the word itself focuses on performing ministry or priestly work.

This word means “new,” describing something that has not previously existed in its present form or has recently come into use. It can identify something fresh, different, or newly established. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 42 times across 36 verses, including expressions concerning new garments, new wine, a new commandment, and what is made new. Its exact force depends on the noun and sentence where it appears, but its central idea remains something new rather than old or previously established.

d: To bend, stoop down, bow the head.

e.t: This word means “to bend down” or “to stoop down.” It describes lowering the upper body, whether by bending forward or bringing oneself closer to the ground. As an action word, it focuses on the physical movement itself rather than explaining the reason for it. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Mark 1:7 and John 8:6, showing the ordinary action of stooping or bending down in two separate passages.

d: (Aramaic), either: Our Lord has come, or: Our Lord comes (will come, is at hand).

e.t: This word means “Come, Lord!” It is an urgent expression calling on the Lord to come. The form “Maranatha” is also used as a rendering of this expression. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both within one verse: 1 Corinthians 16:22. Its concise wording makes it a direct appeal rather than a description or ordinary action. The surrounding verse provides the context for understanding the particular force of the appeal there.

This word means “testimony”: a witness or declared account about what someone knows or has seen. It names what is presented as a true report, whether offered by a person or directed toward others. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 37 times, including repeated use in John, Revelation, and 1 John. Its central idea remains testimony—communicated witness that affirms something as true.

This word refers to deportation or exile—the removal of people from their homeland and their life among another people. It describes a forced displacement rather than an ordinary journey or voluntary move. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, all in Matthew 1, where it names the exile associated with Israel’s history. The related rendering “exile” confirms this central sense. Its precise force in any sentence depends on the surrounding context, but the word itself points to being carried away from one’s homeland.

This word describes someone or something as “one and only” or “unique.” It emphasizes singularity: there is no comparable second one in view. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs nine times, including descriptions of a child and language concerning Jesus. Its central idea is not merely that something is present, but that it holds a singular place as the unique or only one. The surrounding passage determines how that uniqueness is expressed in each verse.

This word describes deep sorrow or mourning—the grief a person feels and expresses in response to loss or painful circumstances. It points to more than ordinary sadness, emphasizing sorrow that weighs heavily on the heart. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, and both occurrences are rendered “mourning.” As a noun-like expression, it identifies the condition or outward expression of profound grief rather than an action performed by someone. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding context, but its central meaning remains deep, expressed sorrow.

d: To deceive, beguile, reason falsely, mislead.

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb means “to deceive”: to lead someone toward a false conclusion or mistaken belief. It describes misleading another person rather than simply being mistaken oneself. The word appears twice in the Greek New Testament, once in Colossians and once in James, so its basic meaning is consistent across both occurrences. The surrounding verse determines whether the deception concerns reasoning, judgment, or conduct, but the central idea remains causing someone to accept what is false.

e.t: This word means “near” or “neighbor,” referring to someone close by or nearby. As a noun, it commonly identifies another person in relation to oneself, especially the person one is called to love. In the New Testament, it is used 17 times and is most often rendered “neighbor.” Its meaning can describe a fellow person without limiting the word to family, friendship, or physical distance. The surrounding sentence determines whether the emphasis is on being nearby or on the person regarded as one’s neighbor.

e.t: This word means to foretell—to predict or tell something beforehand. It describes announcing what will happen before the event occurs, whether the announcement concerns a future circumstance or coming experience. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, each in a different verse, so its basic sense remains consistent across its uses. The surrounding passage determines what is being foretold and why it is mentioned. References include Acts 1:16, 2 Corinthians 13:2, Galatians 5:21, and 1 Thessalonians 3:4.

d: Poor, destitute, spiritually poor, either in a good sense (humble devout persons) or bad.

e.t: This word means “poor,” referring to a person who lacks material wealth or ordinary financial resources. In the New Testament, it is used for people recognized as poor and in need, including those whose limited means are highlighted in teaching or described through their giving. It occurs 34 times in the Greek New Testament, so its basic sense is consistently connected with material poverty rather than abundance. The surrounding passage determines the particular emphasis in each occurrence.

e.t: This word means “to ask” or “to inquire”—to seek information by putting a question to someone. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 12 times, showing a recurring word for seeking knowledge through questions. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on who is asking and what information is being sought.

In the Greek New Testament, it appears five times, including statements about sheep being scattered and people being separated. It can also describe scattering in the broader sense of distributing or spreading something. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis is on separation, dispersal, or distribution. e.t: This word means to agree, or to agree with what has been said. It describes expressing assent rather than merely hearing or considering an idea. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Romans 7:16. Its precise role there depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic sense is agreement with a statement, judgment, or principle. The word therefore points to recognizing something as right or true and affirming it.

e.t: This word means “to converse” or “to talk with,” describing direct spoken interaction between people. It functions as a verb, pointing to the act of speaking with someone rather than naming a person, place, or thing. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 10:27. Its basic sense is simply conversation or personal communication; the surrounding verse determines the particular subject and tone of that conversation.

In the Greek New Testament, it appears six times, including passages addressing personal humility, sober living, and clear-mindedness. Its basic emphasis is a settled and properly ordered mind, though the surrounding verse determines how that quality is expressed in each setting.

This word means a grave or tomb—the place where a dead person is buried. It is a noun used for a burial place, whether referring to tombs generally or to a particular tomb. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs seven times, mostly in Matthew and once in Romans. Its ordinary sense remains concrete: a place associated with burial and the body of the dead.

Its exact force in any passage depends on the surrounding sentence and scene.

This word means “valley,” referring to a lower area of land between hills or mountains. It occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Luke 3:5. The word itself identifies a physical feature of the landscape; its fuller significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the way the verse uses the image. The same meaning is reflected consistently in the available English renderings.

d: (a) the vital breath, breath of life, (b) the human soul, (c) the soul as the seat of affections and will, (d) the self, (e) a human person, an individual.

e.t: This word refers to “life” or “soul.” It can describe the life a person possesses, or the soul understood as the person’s inner, living self. English translations use both “life” and “soul,” so the surrounding sentence determines which sense is clearest. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 103 times, showing that it is a regular word for speaking about human life or the soul rather than a rare or specialized term. It appears from Matthew through Revelation, including passages translated with either “life” or “soul.”
